clue.text: Chemical contents of beer listed

indicators.note: the contents of a word are what lies inside its skin, so only the inner letters of the next word count

blocks.note: the inside of the word beer
items listed come one, then the next

explanation.surface: A label on a bottle shows the chemicals in the beer.
explanation.walkthrough: The two middle letters of beer wrap around THEN, giving ETHENE. Reading 'listed' as THEN (the word that strings a list together) is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethene, also called ethylene, is a simple hydrocarbon gas, an industrial chemical compound.

clue.text: Trying new way of cooking omelettes

indicators.note: a way of cooking eggs reworks them, so the letters of the following word are mixed up

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A cook finds a new method of making omelettes hard going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trying' looks like an attempt at a new recipe, but it is the adjective meaning irritating.
explanation.definitionFit: Nettlesome means irritating or vexing, just as a trying person or situation tests your patience.

clue.text: Lady in sports car is a flapper

indicators.note: a lady sitting in a car is enclosed by it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: GT, gran turismo, labels a sports car
a woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman in a sports car is a 1920s flapper, a fashionable young party girl.
explanation.walkthrough: A flapper was a jazz-age young woman, which suits the lady in the sports car; here it means something that flaps its wings.
explanation.definitionFit: A gannet is a large seabird, and any bird is jokingly something that flaps its wings.

clue.text: Little chap with scales has fat clothing size made thinner

indicators.note: fat clothing something wraps around it, so one piece goes inside the other
making something thinner trims its sides, so the word loses its outside letters

blocks.note: lard is pig fat
the word size without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A small man on a diet weighs himself on the scales and drops a clothing size.
explanation.walkthrough: The scales look like bathroom scales for a slimmer; they are reptile skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A lizard is a small reptile covered in scaly skin, playfully called a little chap.

clue.text: Couple upset one after the other

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset turns a word upside down, so it reads from the bottom
after sets one piece behind the other in the order they are written

blocks.note: a bit of the other is slang for sex, also called it
one, the speaker, is me

explanation.surface: A couple fall out over one partner sleeping with someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The other' is British slang for sex, as in 'a bit of the other', and IT means the same; one (meaning me) is turned over and placed after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people seen together romantically are called an item in gossip columns.

clue.text: E.g. fish with stuffing cooks gently

indicators.note: stuffing goes inside something, so the abbreviation is placed within the verb

blocks.note: W is short for with
to simmer is to cook just below the boil

explanation.surface: A recipe: stuffed fish, poached over a low heat.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen setting makes fish look like food; it is an example of creatures that swim.
explanation.definitionFit: Fish move through water by swimming, so they are an example of swimmers.

clue.text: Tip head right down in water

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending the top letter right down to the bottom moves the first letter to the end

blocks.note: to water down a liquid is to thin it

explanation.surface: Advice to tip your head all the way under the water.
explanation.walkthrough: THIN moves its first letter to the bottom. 'Tip' looks like an instruction to tilt; it is a piece of advice.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip is a useful piece of advice, and a hint is a small suggestion of the same kind.

clue.text: Health worker first wraps up what Patsy takes

indicators.note: the piece that wraps up the sequence comes last, after the other piece

blocks.note: a patsy is a fall guy who takes the rap, the blame
first is written 1ST, with 1 read as I

explanation.surface: A medical professional takes on the burden first, as if absorbing a patient's troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: Patsy looks like a woman's name; with its capital it disguises a patsy, a dupe who takes the rap for others.
explanation.definitionFit: A therapist treats patients' physical or mental conditions, so belongs among health professionals.

clue.text: Kentish beauties order fifth slice and put on weight

indicators.note: to order something is to rearrange it, so the following letters are put in a new sequence
putting on something adds it to what is already there, so one more letter joins the mix

blocks.note: the anagram fodder
W is the abbreviation for weight

explanation.surface: Kentish beauties order a fifth slice of cake and gain weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on weight' adds W to the jumble. Kent is the county at England's south-east corner, home of the chalk cliffs of Dover.
explanation.definitionFit: The white chalk cliffs of Dover in Kent are a famous scenic landmark, a natural beauty of the county.

clue.text: Trip with commission

blocks.note: to trip up is to make a mistake, to err
and means together with

explanation.surface: A business journey paid for on commission.
explanation.walkthrough: Trip looks like a journey, which suits an errand, but it is the verb to slip up.
explanation.definitionFit: An errand is a task one is sent to carry out, a small commission given by someone else.

clue.text: According to report, prestigious school's gone down

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word is taken by its sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: Eton is England's famous elite boarding school

explanation.surface: A news report says a top school's standards or reputation have slipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone down' suggests decline; it means swallowed, as food goes down.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has been eaten has gone down the throat, so the past participle matches.

clue.text: Old school American couple retired amidst change

indicators.note: retired means gone back, so the pair is read backwards
amidst places one piece in the middle of the other

blocks.note: to alter is to change
two lots of AM, short for American

explanation.surface: An elderly American couple, now retired, return to their old school amid changes.
explanation.walkthrough: A couple of AMs gives two of them, which are then turned round inside ALTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Alma mater, Latin for nourishing mother, is the phrase for the school or university one attended.

clue.text: Down but a daughter missing, left plane in a panic

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so that letter is taken out of the word

blocks.note: feeling down is feeling dejected
D is short for daughter

explanation.surface: A miserable pilot without his daughter bails out of a crashing aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: DEJECTED loses its D. 'Down' sits first, looking like part of the plane story; it is the mood.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot who is ejected is propelled out of the aircraft by an emergency seat, typically when it is going down.

clue.text: Maybe take tuppence off assortment of ha'pence

indicators.note: an assortment is a mixed collection, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper knocks a couple of old pennies off a mixed bag of small coins.
explanation.walkthrough: Tuppence (two pence) and ha'pence (halfpennies) are old British small coins.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheapen something is to lower its price, and a small reduction like two pence is one example.

clue.text: Wait until this line has gone if giving a speech

definitions.text: Wait until this line has gone if giving a speech

indicators.note: giving a speech means speaking out, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.clueFragment: Wait until this line has gone
blocks.note: a line of people waiting is something you stand in until it has moved on

explanation.surface: Advice to a speaker to pause until the people in line have gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also describes an actor's prompt: you wait for it, the previous line spoken, before giving your own speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue is the signal, often another actor's last words, that tells a performer to begin speaking.

clue.text: I don't care for the beautiful junk in this pile

definitions.text: I don't care for the beautiful

indicators.note: junk is a jumbled heap of rubbish, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone with no time for beauty dismisses an art collection as a junk heap.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the philistine speaking for themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A philistine is a person indifferent or hostile to art and culture, who cares nothing for beauty.

clue.text: Huge exporter's blue shoes run out once in fashion

indicators.note: out once means one occurrence is dropped, so one copy of that letter goes

blocks.note: blue is the colour of the Conservatives, CON for short
trainers are sports shoes
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run
hip means fashionable

explanation.surface: A big footwear exporter's blue shoes, once fashionable, have sold out.
explanation.walkthrough: TRAINERS has two Rs and loses only one. Blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative party.
explanation.definitionFit: A container ship is a vast cargo vessel that carries goods abroad, a huge carrier of exports.

clue.text: Inclined to pinch hit, he somehow edges sixes

indicators.note: somehow means by some unexplained means, so the letters are arranged anyhow
edges means borders, so the jumbled letters go around the sixes

blocks.note: the anagram fodder
six is VI in Roman numerals, so sixes are VIs

explanation.surface: A cricketer prone to pinching runs slashes edges for sixes.
explanation.walkthrough: Hit, edges and sixes all look like cricket, where an edge is a ball glancing off the bat; none are used that way.
explanation.definitionFit: Thievish means given to stealing, and to pinch is everyday slang for to steal.

clue.text: One has to be generous, parting with a grand

indicators.note: parting with something means giving it up, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: to give freely is to be generous
G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: A donor must be generous enough to hand over a thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One has' reads as part of a moral maxim; it is the definition, the speaker saying I have.
explanation.definitionFit: I've is the contraction of I have, where one means the speaker in formal English.

clue.text: See 9
Most of fleet, I'd expect, that's going out with the wind?

indicators.note: most of the words, not all, are used, so the answer is a stretch inside them

blocks.note: letters running across these words

explanation.surface: A sailor guesses most of the fleet will sail out with the wind behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from the second letter of fleet to the first of expect.
explanation.definitionFit: A lee tide is a tidal current running in the same direction as the wind blows.

clue.text: French pilot swapping sides would be British, by George!

indicators.note: sides are left and right, so the letters for left and right change places

blocks.note: BR is short for British
George Eliot, the Victorian novelist

explanation.surface: A French airman who changed allegiance would be British, by George!
explanation.walkthrough: BR plus ELIOT makes BRELIOT; swap its L and R. 'By George' looks like an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Blériot was the French aviator who made the first aeroplane flight across the English Channel in 1909.

clue.text: Gun directed at parts of northwest France

indicators.note: something that parts the gun splits it open, so the other piece sits inside

blocks.note: the Bren gun, a light machine gun
to means towards

explanation.surface: A gun aimed at parts of Brittany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' looks like regions of France; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Breton describes Brittany, the peninsula region forming the northwest corner of France.

clue.text: Non-resident no longer wasted rent

indicators.note: wasted means ruined, so the word is broken up and its letters rearranged

blocks.note: ex means former
the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A former tenant who no longer lives there feels the rent was wasted.
explanation.walkthrough: An extern is a pupil or worker living outside the institution.
explanation.definitionFit: An extern is someone connected with an institution who lives outside it, such as a day pupil.

clue.text: Returning fast from Paris, one to go through

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the word for fast is written backwards

blocks.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting
un is French for one

explanation.surface: Coming back quickly from Paris, a traveller takes the Channel Tunnel.
explanation.walkthrough: The French one simply sits inside the reversed fast; the Channel Tunnel links Paris and London, so the answer is in the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To tunnel is to dig a way through something, so it means going through it.

clue.text: What it says on the tin

definitions.text: What it says on the tin

blocks.clueFragment: What it says on the tin
blocks.note: surface reading: the British advertising slogan for a product that does exactly what its label promises

blocks.clueFragment: What it says on the tin
blocks.note: setter's reading: the worth printed on a coin, or the apparent meaning of something taken literally

explanation.walkthrough: 'Does exactly what it says on the tin' is a well-known British slogan from Ronseal wood-stain adverts, now an idiom for something being as described.
explanation.definitionFit: Face value is the nominal worth printed on money, or the apparent meaning of something, exactly what it appears to state.

clue.text: Smart electronic device in which power doesn't remain constant

indicators.note: a letter that does not remain is swapped out, with the other one taking its place

blocks.note: a silicon chip
P is the symbol for power
C is a standard symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light

explanation.surface: A sleek gadget whose power supply keeps fluctuating.
explanation.walkthrough: CHIP swaps its P for C. 'Power doesn't remain constant' reads as an electrical fault.
explanation.definitionFit: Chic means stylish and elegant, which is what smart means when describing appearance.

clue.text: Brian left group trying to stay dry crossing river

indicators.note: the group crossing something stretches over it, so it lies around the other letter

blocks.note: L for left
Alcoholics Anonymous helps members stay off drink
R for river

explanation.surface: A man called Brian leaves his support group in their attempt to cross a river without getting wet.
explanation.walkthrough: Brian Lara is the great West Indian cricketer; 'dry' means teetotal, not out of the water.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Lara, the Trinidadian batsman, holds the record Test innings score, so Brian points to his surname.

clue.text: Major satellite contract delivered

indicators.note: a speech is delivered aloud, so the word is used for its sound

blocks.note: to contract is to draw tighter

explanation.surface: A big satellite contract has been fulfilled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a business deal; it is the verb to shrink, and 'delivered' means spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Titan is Saturn's largest moon, a major natural satellite in the solar system.

clue.text: Canvas sacks emptied and refilled with trouble

indicators.note: an emptied word has lost its contents, so only its outer letters stay
refilling puts new contents inside, so the other piece goes into the shell

blocks.note: the first and last letters of sacks
to ail is to trouble

explanation.surface: Canvas sacks are emptied and filled again with some difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canvas' looks like the sacks' fabric; it is the definition, as sailors say of a ship under canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: Canvas is the traditional fabric for sails, so canvas collectively means a ship's sails.

clue.text: Snarled up ring road & English Channel stopping free movement of workers

definitions.text: Channel stopping free movement of workers

indicators.note: traffic snarled up is tangled, so the letters that follow are knotted into a new order

blocks.note: the anagram fodder
E for English

explanation.surface: A jammed ring road and the English Channel both stop workers moving freely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English Channel' is the obvious phrase but it splits: English gives a letter, Channel starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rio Grande is a river forming much of the US-Mexico border, a channel that migrant workers struggle to cross.
